title: Blueberries, Gut Microbiota and Mood: What a New Pilot Study Reveals
metaDescription: A study explored the effects of daily blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome and mood in older adults.
excerpt: A study evaluates how eating blueberries daily for three months could influence gut microbiome enzymes and mood.
imageAlt: A bowl of fresh blueberries on a wooden table in natural light.

blocks.text: Introduction: the link between diet and emotional well-being

In recent years, scientific interest in understanding how food affects the mind has grown substantially. One area of special attention is the gut-brain axis, the communication network that connects the digestive system with the central nervous system. Against this backdrop, researchers have begun to explore whether certain fruits included in the daily diet can influence emotional well-being, particularly in the older adult population.

This concern arises because older adults often face changes in their physical health, reduced activity levels and mood variations. Understanding whether simple nutritional interventions can modify the microorganisms that live in the gut is a promising line of research for public health.
What the source says: findings, participants and limitations of the study

A pilot study carried out by the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife, in collaboration with institutions such as Harvard Medical School, evaluated the effect of daily blueberry consumption in adults aged 65 or older who were physically inactive and had mild depressive symptoms. Dr. Courtney L. Millar, an assistant scientist at the institute and a Harvard professor, led this work, published in The Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging.

The trial used a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-arm design over three months. A total of 18 participants completed the trial: 10 in the group that consumed 48 grams of blueberry powder daily (equivalent to roughly two cups of fresh blueberries) and 8 in the placebo group. Most participants were white women, with an average age of 71 in the blueberry group and 75 in the placebo group.

To assess the changes, the scientists used metagenomic sequencing to analyze microbial species and genes, as well as mass spectrometry to measure short-chain fatty acids in stool. Mood was assessed through validated questionnaires before and after the intervention.

The results showed that participants who consumed blueberries had a larger and more consistent reduction in depressive symptoms. However, when this improvement was compared with the placebo group, the difference was not statistically significant. Likewise, the overall abundance of bacteria and metabolites showed no global changes.

Even so, a statistically significant change was detected within the blueberry group: an increase in the abundance of genes associated with specific microbial enzymes. Among them, the polyamine-transporting ATPase (EC 3.6.3.31) stands out, which is involved in the production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a key neurotransmitter in brain signaling. The authors stress that, because this is a pilot study with a small sample, larger studies are needed to draw definitive conclusions.
Context: fiber, anthocyanins and the gut-brain axis

To understand the relevance of these findings, it is important to consider the makeup of the fruit. Blueberries are known for their dietary fiber and anthocyanins, plant compounds with antioxidant capacity. The hypothesis raised in the study suggests that these components may interact with the gut microbiota and modify metabolites relevant to mood.

Although the overall diversity of microbial species did not change substantially during the trial, the finding about the enzymes suggests that blueberries could influence specific functions of the microbiome without necessarily altering its entire bacterial structure.
What it means for you: practical use without exaggeration

From a practical perspective, these preliminary results offer clues about the importance of including plant-based foods in the daily routine. However, the researchers make clear that these data do not show that blueberries cure or treat depression, nor should they replace treatments prescribed by health professionals.

For those looking to maintain a balanced diet, adding fruits rich in fiber and anthocyanins is a valuable option within a healthy lifestyle. Observations about neurotransmitters such as GABA open interesting paths for science, but everyday application should focus on the overall balance of the diet.

This pilot study provides initial evidence on how nutrition can interact in subtle ways with enzyme activity in the gut of older adults. Although larger-scale research is needed to confirm a direct effect on mood, the findings strengthen scientific interest in the relationship between diet and brain health.
